1254.title: Rising early
1254.hook: the code asks Sikhs to rise early, bathe and remember
1254.howItsDone: Sikhs who keep the code rise in the amrit vela before dawn, bathe, and remember Waheguru before reciting the morning banis; some gurdwaras hold early morning kirtan for those who come.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the daily banis: Japji, Jaap and the Swayyas at morning, Rehras at evening, Sohila at night. Your line was the code's nitnem.

The house is still dark. The street outside hasn't started yet: no buses, no phones buzzing, no one needing anything. Somewhere a tap runs, then stops. A person sits down on a folded blanket with wet hair and a covered head, and begins the first words of the day under their breath. The morning prayers have to start somewhere, and the code says where: before the day starts asking. Get up. Wash. Remember.
screen: `THE HOUSE STILL DARK.` → `A TAP RUNS, THEN STOPS.` → `GET UP. WASH. REMEMBER.`

segments.voice: In paraphrase, the code asks a Sikh to wake in the amrit vela, the ambrosial hour before dawn, to bathe, and, with the mind turned toward the one Immortal Being, to repeat the name Waheguru. The phrase amrit vela isn't new with the code. It comes from Japji Sahib itself, where Guru Nanak says that in the ambrosial hour one should reflect on the true Name and on God's greatness. And Guru Ram Das, the fourth Guru, draws a whole day around it. In his verse in Gauri, paraphrased: whoever calls themselves a Sikh of the true Guru rises early and meditates on the Name; makes the effort in those early hours and bathes; repeats the Name as the Guru teaches; and then, through the day, keeps singing the Guru's word. Notice where the picture ends. Not at dawn. It runs on into the ordinary hours. The early quiet is where the day's direction gets set. Now the second verb: bathe. Japji has a line some readers hear as blunt about what water can't do: cleansing doesn't make the mind pure, even if you wash a hundred thousand times. So the bath isn't the purity. It readies the body. The remembering is the point. Get up, so you're awake for it. Wash, so you're present in your body for it. Then remember, before anything else gets the first word. The order is the teaching: the first thing the day hears is the Name.
screen: `AMRIT VELA, THE HOUR BEFORE DAWN.` · `A SIKH OF THE GURU RISES EARLY.` · `WATER DOESN'T MAKE THE MIND PURE.` · `THE FIRST WORD GOES TO THE NAME.` · then, large: `RISE AND REMEMBER.`

segments.voice: Choose a morning this week and rehearse it now: feet on the floor, cold water on your face, sitting down before the phone gets picked up. Decide what the first word of that day will be, Waheguru said slowly if you pray, or one quiet breath chosen on purpose if not.
Rising early. The code's morning: wake in the amrit vela, bathe, and remember the Name before the day begins. Today's word.
Your line: rise and remember. The quiet before the day starts asking. See you in the morning.

1255.title: Joining the sangat
1255.hook: the code encourages visiting the gurdwara and learning Gurbani together
1255.howItsDone: Sikhs gather in the gurdwara to hear kirtan, listen to explanations of Gurbani and join the Ardas; families often go together, and gurdwaras welcome visitors.

segments.voice: Yesterday, rising early: get up, wash, and give the Name the first word of the day. Your line was rise and remember.

Why does a song you've hummed alone in the car sound different in a room full of people singing it? Alone, you skip the lines you don't know. In the room, someone beside you knows them, and you lean on their voice until you've got it. Somebody hits the high note you were afraid of. Somebody else keeps time. By the end you know the song better, and you can't say exactly who taught you. The Sikh code has a word for that room, and it asks a Sikh not to stay home in the car.
screen: `ALONE IN THE CAR.` → `A ROOM FULL OF VOICES.` → `YOU CAN'T SAY WHO TAUGHT YOU.`

segments.voice: The word is sangat: company, the gathered congregation. In paraphrase, the code says the Guru's word sinks in more readily and more deeply when a Sikh hears it in the sangat, and so it encourages Sikhs to visit the gurdwara and join the congregation there, to listen and to reflect on Gurbani together. Notice what the code is claiming. Not that the gurdwara is the only place the word can be heard; a Sikh has nitnem at home, morning and night. The claim is about depth. Some things you take in better with others in the room. Now, which room? Guru Nanak asks that himself, in Siri Rag. In paraphrase: how is the true company known? Where the One Name alone is spoken of. That's the test. Not the size of the hall, not who built it or who's in charge. A sangat is known by what is said there. So a crowded hall with something else at its center would fail the test, and a few people at a kitchen table reading Gurbani together would pass it. And look at the verbs in the code: hear, reflect, learn. In a sangat one person catches a line another missed. Someone explains a word. A child picks up a melody before she can read it. A newcomer hears a hymn for the first time in the voices of people who've loved it for years. The learning moves sideways, from person to person, not only from the front. Not learn alone, then gather. Learn together.
screen: `SANGAT: THE GATHERED COMPANY.` · `THE WORD SINKS IN MORE DEEPLY.` · `KNOWN BY WHAT IS SAID THERE.` · `LEARNING MOVES SIDEWAYS.` · then, large: `LEARN TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a gathering where something good is learned together, a gurdwara, which is open to visitors of any background, a study group, a table where people read aloud, and picture which day you could go and who might come with you. Your line: learn together. The high note is easier with company. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1256.title: In the gurdwara
1256.hook: no idols, no one seated higher than the Granth, heads covered for all
1256.howItsDone: In the gurdwara, Sikhs and visitors remove their shoes, cover their heads, bow before the Guru Granth Sahib if they choose, and sit on the floor together; the Granth rests on a raised seat under a canopy.

segments.voice: Yesterday, joining the sangat: a company known by what is said there, where learning moves from person to person. Your line was learn together.

Shoes come off at the door, in long rows on racks. Near the entrance, in some gurdwaras, there's a basket of folded head scarves for anyone who arrived without one. Inside, the hall is mostly floor: carpet or white sheets, and people sitting on it, cross-legged, side by side. No pews, no front row of special chairs. At the far end, one thing is raised up, under a canopy, wrapped in cloth. Everything in the room points toward it.
screen: `SHOES OFF, HEADS COVERED.` → `A HALL THAT IS MOSTLY FLOOR.` → `ONE THING RAISED UP.`

segments.voice: Gurdwara means the Guru's door. And the Guru, for Sikhs, is the Guru Granth Sahib, the word. So the code arranges the whole room around a single rule, and it shows up three ways. First: no idols. In paraphrase, the code says no idol or image is to be set up in the gurdwara for worship. What Sikhs bow before there is the Guru Granth Sahib, the written word of the Gurus. Second: no one above the word. The Granth rests on a raised seat under a canopy; the congregation sits on the floor. The code says that sitting on a cushion or a special seat in the Granth's presence, in the sangat, goes against the Guru's way. So a visiting official and the person who swept the hall that morning sit on the same floor, at the same height, facing the same way. The only raised seat in the room belongs to the word. Third: heads covered, for all. Men and women, Sikh or visitor, cover their heads in the Granth's presence. The code also says any person, of any country, religion or caste, may come into the gurdwara. The door is open, and what's asked is the same of everyone who walks through it: shoes off, head covered, sit down on the floor. Put the three together and the room becomes a sentence. Nothing carved stands in for God. No person sits over anyone else. Everyone arrives in the same posture of respect. And in the middle of it all, raised up and honored, is the word.
screen: `GURDWARA: THE GURU'S DOOR.` · `NO IDOLS; THE WORD AT THE CENTER.` · `NO SEAT HIGHER THAN THE GRANTH.` · `HEADS COVERED; THE DOOR OPEN TO ALL.` · then, large: `NO ONE ABOVE THE WORD.`

segments.voice: If you've been inside a gurdwara, walk through it in your mind, the shoe racks, the scarf on your head, the floor under you, the raised seat at the front; if not, use today's picture. Then look around the room you're in now and simply notice what's raised up, and what everything points toward.
In the gurdwara. The Guru's door: no idols, no one seated higher than the Granth, and heads covered for all who enter. Today's word.

1257.title: Opening and resting the Granth
1257.hook: the Granth is opened at dawn and put to rest at night
1257.howItsDone: In gurdwaras the Guru Granth Sahib is opened in the morning with Ardas (prakash) and, after the night prayers, closed, wrapped in rumalas and taken to rest (sukhasan); some families with a Granth at home do the same.

segments.voice: Yesterday, in the gurdwara: no idols, no seat higher than the Granth, heads covered for all. Your line was no one above the word.

Before the sangat arrives, a small group crosses the hall. One person walks in the middle with something wrapped in cloth, held up with great care. Another walks beside, waving a whisk over it. A third waits at the raised seat, smoothing the cloths. For Sikhs, what's being carried is the Guru, and so a strange, tender set of questions follows. Where does the Guru spend the night? Who wakes the Guru up?
screen: `CARRIED ACROSS THE HALL.` → `FOR SIKHS, THE GRANTH IS THE GURU.` → `THE TWO EDGES OF THE DAY.`

segments.voice: The morning word is prakash. In Punjabi it means light, or appearing. In the gurdwara it names the opening of the Guru Granth Sahib for the day. In the early morning the Granth is brought to its raised seat, carried with care, in larger gurdwaras on someone's head. An Ardas is said. The cloths are drawn back. The Granth is opened, and a passage is read from it, a custom coming up soon. For Sikhs, from then on, the Guru is present in the hall. In paraphrase, the code says the Granth should be opened in the gurdwara each day, and not kept closed without good reason. The evening word is sukhasan, a seat of ease, of rest. After the night prayers, the Granth is closed, wrapped in its cloths, called rumalas, and carried to a place of rest, in some gurdwaras its own room. The hall goes quiet. In the morning it all begins again. Look at the shape of that. It's the shape of a day lived by a person: woken gently, present and attended through the hours, then laid down to rest with care at night. Some Sikh families who keep a Granth at home in its own room do the same, morning and night. It's easy to treat a ritual like this as fuss. But the care is the teaching. How you open a thing and how you put it down tell you what it is to you. The word is opened in light, and rested in ease.

segments.voice: Think about how this morning began, whether it was opened or just crashed in, and how you'll lay tonight down. Choose one small act for each edge, a slow breath before you reach for anything, a light turned off on purpose, and if you pray, let the first and last words of the day be the Guru's.

1258.title: What may be sung
1258.hook: only Gurbani and the works of Bhai Gurdas and Bhai Nand Lal are sung in kirtan
1258.howItsDone: In the gurdwara, ragis sing kirtan from Gurbani, sometimes with the works of Bhai Gurdas or Bhai Nand Lal, usually with harmonium and tabla; the words are often shown on a screen for the sangat to follow.

segments.voice: Yesterday, prakash and sukhasan: the Granth opened in light at dawn and rested with care at night. Your line was open and rest.

A harmonium wheezes into its first chord. A tabla player taps the skin twice to check the pitch. Three singers sit cross-legged on a low platform to the side of the Granth, and the hall goes quiet the way a hall does when music is about to start. One question was answered long before anyone sat down. Not which tune. Not which instrument. Which words. The code is strict about it, and the strictness tells you something about what a sung line can do to a person.
screen: `A HARMONIUM'S FIRST CHORD.` → `THE HALL GOES QUIET.` → `NOT WHICH TUNE. WHICH WORDS.`

segments.voice: The singing is called kirtan, the sung praise of God. In paraphrase, the code says that in the sangat, kirtan is to be only of Gurbani, the Gurus' own words, or of the works of Bhai Gurdas and Bhai Nand Lal, which explain Gurbani. That's the whole list. A gifted singer doesn't perform a hymn they wrote last week, however moving it is. A famous poem doesn't get in because it's beautiful. Why draw the line so tight? Go back to the sangat, and Guru Nanak's test: the true company is known by what is said there. A melody is glue for words. A tune can carry a line long after the page is closed. Whatever is sung in the hall is what the sangat will hum in the kitchen, on the drive home, at the hospital bed. So the code guards the words, because the words are what the music will plant. Now the two names on the list. Bhai Gurdas was a Sikh scholar and poet close to the Gurus; tradition calls his writing a key to Gurbani. Bhai Nand Lal was a poet in the Tenth Guru's court, the one met with the poets of Anandpur. Neither is a Guru. Their works are allowed as explanation, so even the exceptions point back to the Guru's word. This is a rule for kirtan in the sangat, not a rule that Sikhs never write or sing anything else. Poetry, folk songs and new music all have their places in Sikh life. But in the hall, in front of the Granth, the voice belongs to the Guru.

1259.title: Taking the hukam
1259.hook: the Granth is opened at random and the first hymn on the left page read
1259.howItsDone: After the Granth is opened in the morning, the granthi opens it at random and reads the hymn at the top of the left-hand page as the hukam; some gurdwaras display it by the door or share it online.

segments.voice: Yesterday, what may be sung: in the sangat, only Gurbani and the works of Bhai Gurdas and Bhai Nand Lal. Your line was only the word.

Nobody picks the page. That's the first thing to know. The Granth has been opened at dawn, and now the reader sits behind it, hands resting on the cloth. The sangat waits. The reader doesn't flip to a favorite hymn or a passage that suits the news. The Granth is opened where it opens. Then the reader's eyes go to one particular place on the page, and whatever is written there is read aloud to everyone in the hall. It has a name, and some gurdwaras write it on a board by the door for anyone who missed it.
screen: `NOBODY PICKS THE PAGE.` → `OPENED WHERE IT OPENS.` → `READ ALOUD TO THE HALL.`

segments.voice: This has come up twice already, with the Tenth Guru's letters and with the one line carried through a day. Today, the method. The word is hukam: order, command. What's read is called the hukam, or the hukamnama, the written order. In paraphrase, the code gives the method. Open the Granth at random. Read the hymn at the top of the left-hand page. If that hymn began on the page before, turn back and read it from its beginning. The hymn is read whole, not cut off where the page happens to start. Why call it an order? Because the word hukam goes back to the very first page of the Granth. Japji Sahib asks how a person can become truthful, how the wall of falsehood can be broken. And it answers, in paraphrase: by walking in the hukam, the Will, which is written along with us. So for Sikhs, hukam isn't a boss's memo. It's the Will that orders everything, the way the tide is ordered and the seasons are. The daily hukam is a small, concrete window onto that: one hymn, received rather than chosen, heard as the Guru's word for this day. It's easy to mistake this for fortune-telling, and that's not how it's understood. The hukam doesn't predict anything. For Sikhs, every page of the Granth is the Guru's word, so wherever it opens, the Guru speaks. What changes is the listening. Some Sikhs read the day's hukam from a gurdwara on their phone before work. Same idea: not a forecast. The order of the day.

1260.title: Three kinds of reading
1260.hook: unbroken, continuous, and the slow sehaj path at your own pace
1260.howItsDone: Sikh families arrange an akhand path, read without a break by a team of readers, for weddings, births, deaths and other occasions; others keep a sehaj path at home, reading the Granth in order at their own pace.

segments.voice: Yesterday, taking the hukam: one hymn, received and not chosen, from the top of the left-hand page. Your line was the order of the day.

A long book can be read the way a marathon is run, or the way a garden is walked. Some people sprint the last chapters at two in the morning because they can't stop. Others leave a bookmark in for a season and come back to it on Sundays. Both finish. They just meet different books along the way. So how do Sikhs read the whole Guru Granth Sahib, from its first page to its last? There's more than one pace for it, and each one has a name.
screen: `A MARATHON, OR A GARDEN WALK.` → `FROM ONE HYMN TO THE WHOLE GRANTH.` → `MORE THAN ONE PACE.`

segments.voice: A path, in Punjabi, is a reading. The first pace is the akhand path. Akhand means unbroken. The whole Granth is read aloud from start to finish without a single pause, by a team of readers taking turns, one handing the line to the next so the voice never stops. Families hold one for a wedding, a birth, a death, a new house, or a hard time. The code speaks to how it should be done: clearly, carefully, with attention, never as background noise. The second pace keeps the reading going in order across set sittings, day after day, so that it finishes in time for an occasion. Continuous, but with rests. And the third is the sehaj path. It has no clock at all. You read the Granth in order, at your own pace, a page or a hymn at a sitting, and you pick up where you stopped. One person can do it alone at home, in whatever time life allows. Now the word sehaj. In Gurbani it names poise, ease, a settled balance of the mind, the calm that comes when a person stops fighting the hukam. So the slow reading is named for the state it hopes to grow. You don't read the Granth fast in order to reach sehaj. You read it in sehaj. And it fits this stretch of the path: rising early, the sangat, the gurdwara's order, the Granth opened and rested, the words that may be sung, the hukam. Each one was about how the word is received. The sehaj path says it can be received at a walking pace too.
screen: `PATH: A READING.` · `AKHAND: UNBROKEN, READERS IN TURN.` · `IN ORDER, WITH RESTS, OR WITH NO CLOCK.` · `SEHAJ: POISE, A SETTLED EASE.` · then, large: `YOUR OWN PACE.`

segments.voice: Choose a text that matters to you, the Granth if it's yours, or any book you've meant to read properly, and be honest about how much you could read at one sitting without rushing: a page, a hymn, a paragraph. Picture where you'd sit, and the bookmark going in at the end of the first sitting.
Sehaj path. A reading of the whole Guru Granth Sahib, in order, at your own pace, named for sehaj, poise and settled ease. Today's word.
Your line: your own pace. The marathon and the garden walk both finish. Same time tomorrow.
